specPoints.text: know what is meant by the terms atom and molecule
know the structure of an atom in terms of the positions, relative masses and relative charges of sub-atomic particles
know what is meant by the terms atomic number, mass number, isotopes and relative atomic mass (Ar)

primer.text: Before starting this note you should already know that all substances are made of particles, that an element contains only one kind of atom, and that a compound joins atoms of different elements together. You met these ideas in Elements, Compounds & Mixtures, along with the difference between mixtures and compounds. If any of those terms feel shaky, revisit that subtopic first, because this note builds directly on it.

lessons.title: The Structure of the Atom
lessons.opening: Every substance around you is built from atoms, and atoms can join into molecules. This lesson covers what those two words mean, what the smaller parts inside an atom are, where each part sits, and why almost all of an atom's mass is packed into its centre. By the end you should be able to state the relative masses and charges of the three particles without your notes.
keyPoints: An atom contains three kinds of sub-atomic particle: protons, neutrons and electrons.
An atom is the smallest particle of an element; a molecule is two or more atoms joined chemically.
Protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus at the centre of the atom, and the nucleus is positively charged.
Electrons race around the nucleus along orbital paths known as shells.
A proton and a neutron each have relative mass 1, while an electron's mass of about 1/1840 is treated as negligible.
Because the electron's mass is negligible, effectively all of an atom's mass is contained in its nucleus.

low.restatement: An atom has a tiny heavy centre and a light outer region, and a molecule is two or more atoms joined into one unit.
low.analogy: Think of a stadium: the nucleus is a handful of coins on the centre spot, and the electrons are dust specks racing around the stands. The coins carry nearly all the weight; the dust barely registers.
low.examPointer: In an exam, say that the mass of an electron is negligible or very small. You are not expected to recall 1/1840, and the note's exam hint says exactly this.

medium.restatement: An atom consists of a nucleus surrounded by electrons in shells. The nucleus holds protons (relative mass 1, charge +1) and neutrons (relative mass 1, charge 0); electrons carry charge -1 and occupy the shells, with relative mass about 1/1840.
medium.analogy: The word relative matters: these values are comparisons between particles, not measurements in grams or coulombs, because sub-atomic particles are far too small for conventional units.
medium.examPointer: Since proton and neutron masses dominate, the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus, which is also why the nucleus's positive charge is what defines the element.

check.stem: Most of the mass of an atom is located in...

options.text: the shells, where the electrons move
options.explanation: The shells hold only electrons, whose mass of about 1/1840 is negligible, so the shells contain almost none of the atom's mass.

options.text: the nucleus, which holds protons and neutrons
options.explanation: Protons and neutrons each have relative mass 1 and both sit in the nucleus, while the electron's mass is negligible, so effectively all the mass is at the centre.

options.text: shared evenly between protons, neutrons and electrons
options.explanation: Electrons are about 2000 times lighter than protons and neutrons, so the mass is not shared evenly.
options.misconception: the phrase relative mass read as equal mass

options.text: the electron orbits considered as a whole
options.explanation: Shells are paths electrons move along, not a store of mass; there is no separate orbit material.

check.stem: Where are the protons and neutrons found in an atom?

options.text: In the nucleus at the centre of the atom
options.explanation: Both heavy particles sit in the nucleus, which is why the centre holds nearly all the mass.

options.text: In shells orbiting the nucleus
options.explanation: Shells belong to the electrons; protons and neutrons never occupy them.

options.text: Spread evenly through the whole atom
options.explanation: The atom has structure: heavy particles at the centre, light ones around the outside.

options.text: Protons in shells, neutrons in the nucleus
options.explanation: Only electrons are found in shells; the nucleus is shared by protons and neutrons alike.

check.stem: What charge does a neutron carry?

options.text: 0 - it is neutral
options.explanation: The neutron is charge-free, which is why it adds mass without affecting charge.

options.text: +1, like the proton
options.explanation: That is the proton's charge; the neutron is the neutral partner in the nucleus.

options.text: -1, like the electron
options.explanation: Negative charge belongs to the electrons in the shells, not to anything in the nucleus.
That mixes up charge with the electron's tiny relative mass.

options.text: Two or more atoms chemically joined into an identifiable unit
options.explanation: The joined unit keeps the properties and composition of the substance it belongs to.

options.text: The smallest particle of an element
options.explanation: That is the atom; the molecule is the joined group of atoms.

options.text: Any particle found in the nucleus
options.explanation: Nuclear residents are protons and neutrons; molecules are built from whole atoms.

options.text: A charged group of particles
options.explanation: Charge is not part of the definition; molecules are about atoms joined together.

check.stem: Why do chemists use relative masses instead of grams for sub-atomic particles?

options.text: The particles are far too small for conventional units, so masses are compared with each other
options.explanation: Relative values are comparisons, not absolute measurements in grams or coulombs.

options.text: Grams are not part of the periodic table
options.explanation: The table lists numbers, but the reason for relative masses is particle size, not the table.

options.text: Because relative masses are exact measured values
options.explanation: They are comparisons between particles, not precise measurements of each one.

options.text: Because electrons would otherwise weigh nothing at all
options.explanation: Electrons do have a tiny mass, about 1/1840 of a proton's; it is small, not zero.

lessons.title: Key Terms and Counting Particles
lessons.opening: Two numbers describe any atom: the atomic number, which counts protons, and the mass number, which counts protons and neutrons together. From those two you can work out every particle count, and compare atoms of the same element that differ in neutron count. The periodic table prints both numbers, so telling them apart is a skill worth practising.
keyPoints: The atomic number counts protons in the nucleus, and in a neutral atom it counts the electrons too.
The mass number counts protons plus neutrons, and it is always the bigger of the two numbers.
Neutron count comes from taking the atomic number away from the mass number.
Isotopes share an element and proton count but differ in their neutron counts.
Relative atomic mass averages an element's isotope masses, weighted by the abundance of each isotope.
Lithium, with atomic number 3 and mass number 7, holds 3 protons, 3 electrons and 4 neutrons.

low.restatement: Read the two printed numbers: the smaller one counts protons, the bigger one counts protons and neutrons together. Take the smaller from the bigger for neutrons, and remember the electron count matches the proton count.
low.analogy: MASS = MASSIVE works like luggage tags: the heavier suitcase wears the bigger number, so the large tag is the mass number and the small one is the atomic number.
low.examPointer: For particle-count questions, write all three counts out - protons from the atomic number, electrons equal to them, neutrons by subtraction - before answering.

medium.restatement: The atomic number gives protons, and neutrality makes electrons match it, so lithium with atomic number 3 has 3 of each. The mass number gives protons plus neutrons, so neutrons are the difference - 7 take away 3 leaves 4. Isotopes keep the proton count but vary neutrons, and relative atomic mass averages an element's isotopes by abundance.
medium.analogy: Picture the periodic table entry as an identity card: the smaller number is the fixed surname, while the bigger number can shift between isotopes, like a recorded weight that varies between siblings.
medium.examPointer: Relative atomic mass questions hinge on the word average: state that isotope masses are weighted by abundance, and quote carbon-12 as the reference standard.

check.stem: An atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many electrons does it hold?

options.text: 11, because a neutral atom matches electrons to its proton count
options.explanation: Atoms are neutral, so the electron count equals the proton count, which the atomic number gives.

options.text: 23, taken from the mass number
options.explanation: Mass number counts protons and neutrons in the nucleus; neither of those sets the electron count.
options.misconception: mass number read as electron source

options.text: 12, to balance the neutrons
options.explanation: Neutrons carry no charge, so nothing needs balancing against them.

options.text: 34, the two numbers added together
options.explanation: Adding the numbers double-counts the protons, and electrons are not part of either figure.

check.stem: For that same atom, how many neutrons does the nucleus hold?

options.text: 12, found by 23 - 11
options.explanation: Neutrons are the mass number minus the atomic number: 23 - 11 = 12.

options.text: 11, the same as the proton count
options.explanation: Protons and neutrons are both counted in the mass number, but they are not equal by definition.

options.text: 23, the whole mass number
options.explanation: That ignores the 11 protons already included in the mass number.
options.misconception: mass number taken as neutron count

options.text: 34, the sum of both numbers
options.explanation: Summing counts the nucleons twice; the question needs a subtraction.
options.misconception: addition used where subtraction is needed

check.stem: Two atoms each carry 6 protons, but one has 6 neutrons and the other 8. What are they?

options.text: Isotopes of the same element
options.explanation: Equal proton numbers mean one element; the differing neutrons make them isotopes of it.

options.text: Atoms of two different elements
options.explanation: Element identity is fixed by proton count, which is equal here.
options.misconception: neutron count taken to change the element

options.text: A molecule split into two atoms
options.explanation: No bond is involved; these are two separate atoms of one element.

options.text: One charged atom and one uncharged atom
options.explanation: Neutron count does not touch charge; that job belongs to the electrons.

check.stem: Which statement about the mass number is correct?

options.text: It counts protons plus neutrons and is always the larger printed number
options.explanation: The exam hint says MASS = MASSIVE: the mass number is the bigger of the two.

options.text: It counts only the protons
options.explanation: That is the atomic number; the mass number adds the neutrons in.
options.misconception: mass number collapsed to atomic number

options.text: It includes the electrons in the shells
options.explanation: Electron mass is negligible, so electrons are left out of the count.

options.text: It is fixed for every atom of an element
options.explanation: Isotopes of one element carry different mass numbers.

check.stem: What does relative atomic mass account for that a plain mass number does not?

options.text: The abundance of every isotope of the element
options.explanation: It is the average mass of one atom, weighted by how common each isotope is.

options.text: The charges of the sub-atomic particles
options.explanation: Charge is a separate property; relative atomic mass is about mass alone.

options.text: The mass of the electrons in the shells
options.explanation: Electron mass is negligible and never drives the average.

options.text: The neutrons of the commonest isotope only
options.explanation: All isotopes and their abundances enter the average, not just one.
options.misconception: average reduced to a single isotope

glossary.definition: The smallest particle of an element, with electrons around a nucleus of protons and neutrons.
Two or more atoms chemically joined into an identifiable unit.
The positively charged centre of an atom where the protons and neutrons are located.
An orbital path around the nucleus in which electrons move.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Atoms of the same element with equal proton counts but different neutron counts.
The average mass of one atom of an element, weighted by isotope abundance.

workedExample.prompt: Determine the number of protons, electrons and neutrons in an atom of element X with atomic number 29 and mass number 63.
steps: The number of protons of element X is the same as the atomic number, so the number of protons = 29.
The number of protons is always equal to the number of electrons, so the number of electrons = 29.
The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the atomic number: 63 - 29 = 34.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Element X has 29 protons, 29 electrons and 34 neutrons.
